title: Drummers should keep the tempo, not play to the public
summary: Greene says the rhythm should follow Basie's tempo start to finish and that the public ruins drummers by wanting a show.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: As long as the drummer's -- when Basie starts a number off -- from whatever tempo he starts off, you know I usually -- I take it from Basie, more or less, you know. And, I think the rhythm

should go according to that, and from start to finish, in other words. Without varying the tempo one way or another. And, I think drummers should follow this pattern all the way through. Even if they -- they can take breaks, or whatever. But, whatever tempo that they leave, they should come right back at that same -- right back on that same beat, in other words.
Right.

But, drummers today -- there are some good drummers, and some bad ones. As far as playing with the band is concerned, we've got some good drummers. We've had some good drummers in there. Some very good drummers. As I say, they -- as far as playing with the band -- they know what they're supposed to do -- dynamics and what-not, and whether or not they should keep it going. I think they should keep the rhythm going right from the start to the finish. And, as I say, we've had some good drummers, and we had some bad ones. But, as of today -- they seem to be working out pretty well. There's a new, you know, a new breed of drummers nowadays than there was way back.
They feel they have to play a bigger role, huh?

Yeah. They -- and it's not a really hard job in this band to play the drums. You know, anybody comes in there that think they have to do an awful lot -- they don't have to. The main thing is to keep the tempo going. That's the main thing. And, whatever they do -- they can play all the breaks they want to, but I mean -- the fill-ins and what-not. That's okay. But, you have to come back to that beat. You can't forget and get too carried away with your breaks.
And mess up?
And, you know what I mean, and forget where you just left, you see.
Right.

And, in a sense, it's really an easy job. It's not no hard thing and they think it's -- you know -- they think they got to do a whole lot of things and play loud and "okay, you can be a show drummer". That's good too, you know.
I was going to say -- in some cases perhaps the worst drummer is nevertheless been most appreciated by the public.
Yeah. Well, you see, that's what I'm saying. The public is -- the public really ruins a drummer. They're the ones. They are responsible for really --
they want an act, a show.
They want a show -- and the louder you play -- you know what I mean -- it's really a shame.
Everybody walks off the stand when the drummer goes into his act.

You see, and I think the drummer should realize this fact, and you know, like, throw the public -- throw them out of your mind. You know -- I mean while you're up there on the bandstand you're playing what's going on, and then afterwards, then you can -- you know. But while you're there -- ignore it -- really. You know, I mean, get the job done while you're up there, you see.
Yeah. To be there for what you're there for.
Right. For what you're there for. I mean, you look out and see the audience and-- how are they going to concentrate on
what's going on up here if they're up there looking out -- "Everybody's watching me" -- you know.
Yeah.
You know -- and forgetting about the work at hand.
